paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Methane is a chemical compound whose formula is CH₄: each molecule has four hydrogen atoms joined to one carbon atom. It is the simplest of the alkanes and the chief ingredient of natural gas. As an organic hydrocarbon, it is one of the simplest organic compounds there are. At standard temperature and pressure it is a gas with no colour and no smell, and you can see through it.

paragraphs.heading: A greenhouse gas
paragraphs.text: In Earth's atmosphere, methane lets visible light through but absorbs infrared radiation, so it acts as a greenhouse gas. Once it reaches the surface and the air, it goes by the name atmospheric methane. It does take in a little visible light, mostly at the red end of the spectrum, but this only shows over a very long path. That is why Uranus and Neptune look blue or blue-green: light travels through their methane-bearing atmospheres and is scattered back out.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: Natural methane lies both underground and beneath the seafloor, and it is made by geological as well as biological processes. The biggest reservoir of all is methane clathrates, buried beneath the seafloor. Methane has also turned up on other planets, Mars among them, which matters for astrobiology research.

paragraphs.heading: A fuel that is hard to hold
paragraphs.text: There is so much methane on Earth that it makes an economically attractive fuel. Catching and storing it is hard, though, because it is a gas at standard conditions: its boiling point is −161.5 °C at one atmosphere of pressure. Mixed with air at standard pressure, it can catch fire anywhere between 5.4% and 17%. The smell of gas in homes is added on purpose for safety, using an odorant that is usually a blend containing tert-butylthiol.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and solid forms
paragraphs.text: A methane molecule is tetrahedral, with four equivalent C–H bonds. Frozen solid, methane is known in nine different forms. Cooling it at normal pressure gives the form called methane I, which crystallizes in the cubic system. In methane I the hydrogen atoms have no fixed positions, so the molecules can turn freely, which makes it a plastic crystal.

paragraphs.heading: How it reacts
paragraphs.text: Methane's main reactions are combustion, steam reforming to syngas, and halogenation, and in general they are hard to control. Some enzymes, called methane monooxygenase, turn methane into methanol (CH₃OH). One group of bacteria oxidises methane using nitrite in place of oxygen, which is known as anaerobic oxidation of methane. Industry, by contrast, has never made large-scale oxidation of methane pay.
